chain.g: a wing (appendage of an animal's body that enables it to fly)

ety.text: From Middle English ele, from Anglo-Norman ele (“wing”) (Modern French aile), from Latin āla (whence English ala). Further from Latin axis (whence English axis, atelier). Via Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- cognate with English axle, Ancient Greek ἄξων (áxōn) (whence English axo-, axon). The modern pronunciation has been influenced by English isle, whence the obsolete form isle; the modern spelling reflects further modification of this form after modern French aile.

senses.d: A wing of a building, notably in a church separated from the nave proper by piers.
A clear path/passage through rows of seating.
A clear corridor in a supermarket with shelves on both sides containing goods for sale.
Any path through an otherwise obstructed space.
Seat in public transport, such as a plane, train or bus, that's beside the aisle.
ex: Do you want to seat window or aisle?

senses.d: An idiomatic divide between the Republican Party and the Democratic Party, who are said to be on two sides of the aisle.
The path of a wedding procession in a church or other venue; (by extension, metonymic) marriage.

Proto-Indo-European *peth₂-der. Proto-Italic *pattus Latin passus Old Spanish passo Spanish paso From Old Spanish passo, from Latin passus, -um (“step, pace”). Cognate with Catalan pas, English pace and pass, French pas, Galician paso, Portuguese passo, and Romanian pas.
